paragraphs.heading: Liquid that moves itself
paragraphs.text: Capillary action is a liquid travelling through a narrow space on its own, with no help from an outside force such as gravity. It also goes by names like capillarity, capillary rise and wicking. You can watch it as liquid climbs between the hairs of a paint brush, up a thin straw, or into porous materials such as paper and plaster. The name comes from the Latin capillaris, meaning like a hair, because a capillary has a tiny diameter, as thin as a hair.

paragraphs.heading: The forces behind it
paragraphs.text: The cause is the pull between molecules of the liquid and the surfaces around it. Two pulls work together. One is surface tension, which comes from cohesion inside the liquid; the other is adhesion between the liquid and the wall of its container. When a tube is narrow enough, the pair drive the liquid along. Adhesion drags the column up the inner wall until there is enough liquid for its weight, pulled by gravity, to win.

paragraphs.heading: Why narrow tubes pull higher
paragraphs.text: Put the bottom of a glass tube in water and the surface inside forms a curve called a concave meniscus. The rim where the top of the column touches the tube grows in step with the tube's radius. The weight of the column, though, grows with the square of the radius. So a narrow tube can lift liquid further than a wide one, as long as the molecules in the middle hold on well enough to those at the edge.

paragraphs.heading: When it runs backwards
paragraphs.text: Liquids do not always climb. With some pairs, such as mercury and glass, the liquid pulls on itself more strongly than it pulls on the solid. The surface then bulges into a convex meniscus, and capillary action works in reverse.

paragraphs.heading: From Leonardo to Einstein
paragraphs.text: Leonardo da Vinci made the first recorded observation of the effect. In 1660 the Irish chemist Robert Boyle still treated it as a novelty. He dipped a thin tube in red wine and put it under a partial vacuum, and the wine's height did not visibly change, so he decided something other than what drives a mercury barometer was at work. A successful mathematical account arrived in 1805, when Thomas Young in Britain and Pierre-Simon Laplace in France derived the Young–Laplace equation. Albert Einstein's first paper, submitted in 1900, was on capillarity.

paragraphs.heading: In towels, pens and eyes
paragraphs.text: Paper towels and sponges soak up spills this way, and the small pores of a sponge behave like tiny capillaries. Some fabrics are said to wick sweat away from the skin, named after the wicks of candles and lamps. A fountain pen uses the effect to draw ink from its cartridge or reservoir to the tip of the nib. In your own body, it drains the tear fluid that your eyes produce all the time.

paragraphs.heading: In soil and walls
paragraphs.text: In the ground, capillary action moves water from wet parts of the soil to dry parts. In buildings, the same effect lies behind rising damp in concrete and masonry. One handy use is the capillary siphon: a soaked cotton cord runs from a raised reservoir of water down into a lower vessel, with no hollow tube needed.
